timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I use PowerShell for basic admin stuff. How is it a security tool?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: PowerShell is the most powerful tool on Windows, Peter. It has direct access to the .NET framework, Windows APIs, and WMI. It can do anything - and attackers love it because it's already installed everywhere.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Exactly. That's why it's called a living-off-the-land tool. The SolarWinds attackers used PowerShell to move through entire networks without dropping a single file on disk. They executed everything in memory.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: PowerShell logging is your first defense. Enable Module Logging, Script Block Logging, and Transcription. These capture every command, even encoded ones. Without logging, PowerShell is invisible.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Constrained Language Mode restricts access to dangerous .NET types. AppLocker can block unsigned scripts. JEA - Just Enough Administration - limits what commands can be run. And AMSI - the Antimalware Scan Interface - lets AV inspect PowerShell scripts before execution.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Attackers bypass these regularly. AMSI bypasses are a cat-and-mouse game. They use encoded commands, downgrade to PowerShell 2.0, or use reflectively loaded .NET assemblies. That's why logging and monitoring matter more than prevention.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Master Get-Process, Get-EventLog, Invoke-Command, and Get-WmiObject. Then learn remote management with PSRemoting and WinRM. For blue team, learn PowerShell forensics with Get-WinEvent and module logging analysis.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Interview tip: explain how PowerShell can be used offensively and defensively, describe AMSI and how attackers bypass it, and list essential logging configurations. Windows security roles always ask this.
